articles.title: Claude Code hooks for teams: four hooks worth committing to your repo
articles.summary: Most teams start shaping Claude Code with instructions: a CLAUDE.md file that says "run the formatter," "never edit the lockfile," "use our logger." That works most of the time. But an instruction is something the model chooses to follow. On a long session, or a busy day, it sometimes doesn't. Hooks close that gap. A hook is a shell command that Claude Code runs automatically at a fixed point, such as after every file edit or before every command. It runs every time, whether or not the model remembers the rule. For a team, that changes what you can promise. "The agent should format its code" becomes "the agent's code is always formatted." Where team hooks live Hooks go in the same settings files as permissions. For a team, the one that matters is .claude/settings.json in the repository, committed like any other config. articles.title: What a LongMemEval Score Does and Doesn't Tell You About Memory for Coding Agents
articles.summary: The LongMemEval benchmark is a public test of long-term memory in chat assistants. It has 500 hand-written questions, and each one sits on top of a long history of past chat sessions between a user and an assistant. To answer a question, a system has to find the right facts in that history and reason over them. The facts may be spread across sessions, may have changed over time, or may not exist at all. The test was published in 2024 and comes in two common sizes. LongMemEval-S gives each question a history of roughly 115,000 tokens. LongMemEval-M uses far larger histories, well beyond what fits in any model's context window. It has become the standard way to compare memory systems for AI assistants. At Open Agentic Brain & Memory (OpenAB), we report a LongMemEval score too. The OpenAB project page lists 94.2% on LongMemEval-S while reading 75% fewer tokens, measured over all 500 questions with a Claude reader. Turn on Push when actions required in /config and permission prompts and questions arrive as pushes. Then you close the MacBook lid, and the session goes quiet. Why The session runs on your Mac. Remote Control is a window into it, not a copy of it. When the Mac sleeps, Claude stops. The docs say exactly this: if your laptop sleeps or your network drops, Claude Code reconnects automatically when your machine comes back online. So it reconnects afterwards. Nothing runs while the Mac is asleep, and the message you sent from your phone waits until the lid opens again. What Is Apache Iggy and Why It Exists Can you tell us a bit about Apache Iggy? Apache Iggy is a persistent message streaming platform written in Rust. It stores messages in streams, topics, and partitions as an append-only log, while consumers read independently or through consumer groups. The server is distributed as a single binary with no external broker or database dependency. It supports TCP, QUIC, WebSocket, and HTTP, and provides SDKs for Rust, C#, C++, Java, Go, Python, Node.js, and PHP. articles.title: From Prompt Injection to Data Leak: Agentic AI Risks
articles.summary: When people talked about AI, the focus in most places was on things like model quality, speed, context window. As of today, the topics being discussed have changed a bit. Now these are the questions being asked more often: What does it have access to? What can it do on its own? What information could it leak? This is exactly where what's called agentic AI comes in. It can read email. It can search for files inside a repo. It can check the calendar. It can make API calls. And this is where the risk begins. In the Global Cybersecurity Outlook 2026 report, 94 percent of respondents say AI will be the factor that changes cybersecurity the most throughout 2026. 87 percent also say that AI-related vulnerabilities are among the fastest-growing risks. That's why it wouldn't be right to talk about agent security as just a trend. Organizations are seeing a new attack surface. So what exactly is the problem? Prompt injection. articles.title: Is flisk.sh a Small CLI or a Big Thing?
articles.summary: People keep asking the wrong size question about flisk.sh. Is it a platform? A Kubernetes replacement? A new way to build companies? No. It is a CLI. You write a service.json, you run flisk up (the GitHub README still says tdk up for the same package), and it generates the local Docker and Tilt wiring so those services start on your machine. Production stays on Helm. That is the whole product sentence, and it is a small sentence on purpose. The interesting question is not whether the binary is big. It is whether the mess it refuses to own is big.
